nameStory: The metallic crab spider gets its name from the males' stunning shiny, metallic appearance that catches light like polished chrome or copper. The 'crab' part comes from their sideways scuttling movement and ability to walk sideways and backwards, just like their ocean-dwelling namesakes.
description: This fascinating running crab spider is a master of disguise with dramatically different looks between males and females. Males sport a smooth, shiny metallic sheen that gleams in sunlight, while females are covered in bristly hairs and colored in muted white and grey tones. They're active hunters that don't build webs to catch prey, instead relying on speed and stealth to ambush insects.

idTips.label: Sexual Differences
idTips.description: Males have a smooth, mirror-like metallic surface that feels sleek to the touch, while females are fuzzy with bristly hairs that feel rough like a tiny bottle brush

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Flattened, crab-like body with front legs held wide like a boxer's stance, allowing them to scuttle sideways with surprising speed

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Runs in quick bursts with sudden stops, often moving sideways or backwards when threatened, never building a web

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Females show mottled grey and white patterns that blend with bark texture, while males appear uniformly metallic with minimal patterning

habitat: Look for these spiders on tree bark, fence posts, and wooden structures where they hunt for small insects. They prefer sunny spots on rough-textured surfaces like oak or pine bark where their coloration provides excellent camouflage. You might also spot them on garden sheds, decks, or stone walls where they can quickly dart into crevices.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, with males beginning their search for mates and showing off their metallic shine in the increasing sunlight.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when both sexes are most visible hunting during daylight hours. This is the best time to observe the dramatic differences between metallic males and bristly females.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues but begins to slow as they prepare for winter. Mated females may be seen guarding egg sacs tucked under bark or in protected crevices.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically die off, with eggs overwintering in protected locations like deep bark crevices or under loose tree bark.

funFact: The male's metallic shine isn't just for show - it's actually caused by special microscopic scales that reflect light like tiny mirrors, making them look like living jewelry when sunlight hits them at the right angle!
confusionNotes: The bristly grey females can be confused with other female running crab spiders, but no other species has males with that distinctive mirror-like metallic finish. Memory trick: 'Marx' sounds like 'marks' - and the metallic male definitely marks this species as special!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'crab spiders,' these running crab spiders are quite different from the sit-and-wait ambush crab spiders (like goldenrod crab spiders) that many people know. Running crab spiders are active hunters that chase down their prey rather than waiting motionless on flowers.
compareHints: Unlike its cousin the White-striped Running Crab Spider which has obvious white stripes, the metallic crab spider males are uniformly shiny without stripes. The Turf Running Spider tends to stay closer to the ground in grass, while metallic crab spiders prefer vertical surfaces like tree bark and posts.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The white-striped running crab spider is distinguished from its relatives by those prominent longitudinal white stripes - most other Philodromus species in New England have more subtle markings or different color patterns.

The Turf Running Spider differs from its Philodromus relatives primarily in habitat preference - while the Metallic Crab Spider tends toward trees and the White-striped Running Crab Spider prefers taller shrubs, the Turf Running Spider sticks to low vegetation and ground cover.

Compared to other Philodromus species in New England, the Resplendent Running Crab Spider stands out for its particularly brilliant metallic appearance - more lustrous than the Metallic Crab Spider and lacking the white stripes of the White-striped Running Crab Spider.

Among its Philodromus relatives in New England, the male's distinctive shiny black coloration with white edges makes it relatively easy to distinguish from the more uniformly colored Metallic Crab Spider or the striped patterns of the White-striped Running Crab Spider.
The Minute Running Crab Spider is significantly smaller than its relatives like the Metallic Crab Spider or White-striped Running Crab Spider, which are much more commonly encountered.
Philodromus exilis is notably more slender than the Metallic Crab Spider or White-striped Running Crab Spider, lacking the metallic sheen or distinct striping of those relatives.
